data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Checklists are not necessarily diagnostic; they could be generative or heuristic.","Non-expert panels can aggregate diverse perspectives, potentially accessing more features than a single expert.","The outcome in clinical judgment is often subjective; here it is objectively verifiable."],"overturn_conditions":["If the panel outperforms the expert on items requiring tacit features, the expert's intuition is not superior, and the claim is false.","If the checklist can be dynamically updated to include new features, the panel's boundedness is temporary.","If the expert's 'tacit' features are actually just noise or bias, the expert's success on those items is spurious."],"shared_structure":["Both involve a conflict between an explicit, rule-based system and an intuitive, holistic system.","Both assume the intuitive system captures features the explicit system cannot.","Both predict the intuitive system wins on complex, high-cue tasks and loses on simple, measurable tasks."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_008"],"transfer_claims":["Just as clinical algorithmic models fail to capture holistic case features that experts use, checklist panels fail to capture tacit outcome features.","The systematic co-failure of the panel on items where the expert succeeds is analogous to the statistical model's failure on outlier clinical cases.","The distinction between the explicit checklist's feature space and the expert's tacit feature space maps to the actuarial vs. clinical judgment divide."]},"claim":"The claim is generally false: a trained non-expert panel with a checklist will not reliably outperform a single domain expert relying on intuition, because the expert's tacit feature recognition operates on a richer, higher-dimensional feature space than any explicit checklist can encode. The single evaluation can distinguish mere compliance from a true gain by testing for systematic co-failures: panels will systematically err on items requiring tacit cues the checklist omits, whereas experts will succeed on those items, proving the panel's performance is checklist-bounded.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the checklist is genuinely complete for the task domain, the expert's tacit knowledge adds no value, and the panel's structured process may win.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the panel's deliberation allows them to collectively infer tacit cues not listed, they are not bound by the checklist's explicit limit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's intuition is poorly calibrated or biased, the tacit features may be misused, and the structured panel may outperform despite the feature deficit.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task is simple and low-dimensional, the checklist may capture all relevant features, making the expert's advantage negligible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Expert intuition is a form of sophisticated pattern recognition honed by experience, capable of integrating weak, implicit, and interacting cues that resist explicit codification. A checklist, by definition, restricts the decision to a pre-specified, low-dimensional subset of features. The panel cannot access the omitted features, so their accuracy is bounded by the checklist's coverage. When the outcome depends on an omitted cue, the panel will systematically fail while the expert succeeds.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
